summary.text: The siege of Jerusalem lasted from 7 June to 15 July 1099 and marked the successful end of the First Crusade.
Christian forces from Western Europe, mobilised by Pope Urban II after the Council of Clermont, attacked a city held first by the Seljuk Turks and later by the Egyptian Fatimids.
After an unsuccessful first attack on 13 June, the crusaders built several siege engines, including a siege tower and a battering ram, and entered the city on 15 July.

facts.label: Failed assault
facts.value: The first attack, on 13 June, was unsuccessful

facts.label: City walls
facts.value: Four kilometres long, three metres thick, 15 metres high

facts.label: Defenders
facts.value: Roughly a thousand troops plus 400 Egyptian elite cavalry

facts.label: Aftermath
facts.value: Thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred

items.prompt: Steep valleys guarded Jerusalem on the east, southeast and west. Where did the terrain favour an attack?

options.label: The eastern side, above the Kidron Valley
The western side, beside the Tyropeon Valley
The southeastern side, above the Hinnom Valley
Along the northern wall and the southwest, over Mount Zion

items.explain: Only the southwest, over Mount Zion and along the entire northern wall, offered terrain favourable for an attack.

items.prompt: Jerusalem's governor expects flying rocks from the crusaders' machines to damage his stone walls. What does he order?

options.label: Straw-filled bags lowered on ropes beside the walls to soften the blows
Wet animal hides nailed over the walls to soften the blows
Sand-filled sacks piled inside the gates to soften the blows
Wooden screens hung from the towers to soften the blows

items.explain: The governor ordered bags filled with straw to be placed beside the walls and lowered on ropes to buffer the impact of flying rocks.

items.prompt: The crusaders' first assault on 13 June had some early success but failed. What lesson did it teach?

options.label: A prophecy was enough to take the city
They needed more siege engines
A longer wait would bring the defenders out
The city's walls could be undermined with ease

items.explain: Despite initial success the attack failed, demonstrating the need for more siege engines.

items.prompt: The crusaders camped outside Jerusalem suffered thirst, while the people inside did not. Why?

options.label: The city stood beside a river that never ran low
The crusaders refused to drink from local wells
The governor spoiled outside supplies, while the city drew on deep cisterns
The city was supplied by sea through the port of Jaffa

items.explain: The governor saw to it that no water was available near the city and most wells and cisterns were made unusable, while the people of Jerusalem drew water from deep cisterns.

items.prompt: The crusaders had too few men to surround all of Jerusalem. What did their leaders do?

options.label: Concentrated on sectors where they could approach the walls
Spread evenly around the whole wall
Waited at Nicaea for reinforcements
Sent tribute to the governor of the city

items.explain: Since they had insufficient forces to besiege the entire city, the crusaders concentrated their strength on the sectors where they could approach the walls.

items.prompt: On the march south along the coast in 1099, how did the crusaders deal with heavily fortified cities?

options.label: They stormed each one in turn until it fell
They struck deals with local Muslim rulers or paid tribute
They left garrisons to starve out each one
They sailed past them with the help of ships

items.explain: Following the coastline, the troops avoided protracted sieges of heavily fortified cities, instead concluding agreements with local Muslim rulers or paying tribute.
